lessons.title: What did you do yesterday? The Perfekt with haben
lessons.goal: Say what you did with haben + a participle, and ask a friend Was hast du gemacht?

grammar.point: The Perfekt is a bracket: haben is part 2 and the past participle is last. A regular participle is ge + stem + t.
grammar.oneLine: Ich habe gestern Tennis gespielt. Was hast du gemacht?

mistake.why: The participle goes to the very end of the sentence, after everything else.

terms.meaning: the form you use to say what happened: Ich habe gespielt
haben in part 2 of a Perfekt sentence
the verb form at the end, for example gemacht or gespielt
helper verb in part 2 and the participle at the end, like kann ... spielen

cards.title: Before we start: what did you do yesterday?
cards.body: Chapter 10 is about study and work: telling what happened, applying for a job and phoning. Today: say what you did yesterday. You know a bracket from Ich muss arbeiten: the second verb waits at the end. The Perfekt is the same bracket, with haben.

examples.why: You know this already: muss + a verb at the end.
New today: habe + a participle at the end.

steps: You already know: the verb bracket, e.g. Ich muss arbeiten and Ich kann Tennis spielen (chapter 5)
New today: the Perfekt = habe (part 2) + a participle at the end, e.g. gespielt
By the end you can: say six things you did and ask a friend Was hast du gemacht?
cards.more: Think of a sentence as a parcel with a handle at each end. In Ich muss arbeiten the handle muss sits in the second place, and arbeiten waits at the very end. The Perfekt is the same parcel: habe in the second place and the participle at the end. Perfekt is only the name of the form we use to say what happened. You do not need to learn it all now. In the next cards you build it step by step, with ten small verbs.

cards.title: Two ways to talk about before
cards.body: You know war and hatte from chapter 6: Ich war gestern müde. They only work for sein and haben. Every other verb uses a new form, the Perfekt: Ich habe gestern Tennis gespielt. Today you only see the idea. The full rule comes later.

examples.why: war: the old way, only for sein.
A chunk for now: learn it whole. A later card explains it.

cards.more: Imagine two doors to the past. The small door is war and hatte: it only opens for sein and haben. The big door is the Perfekt, and all other verbs walk through it. When you are not sure which door to use, ask yourself: is the verb sein or haben? If not, use the Perfekt. In today's lesson you learn the Perfekt with haben, and the question Was hast du gestern gemacht? is a good sentence to remember whole.
cards.lead: You just met the idea of Perfekt in the introduction. On this card: when to use war and hatte and when to use the new form, so you can pick the right way to talk about yesterday.

deeper.text: English does the same: I was and I had are short forms, but for most verbs we say I have played or I played. In German spoken talk, the Perfekt is the normal way to say what happened. You will hear it every day in shops, at work and on the phone.

cards.title: The Perfekt is a bracket
cards.body: The Perfekt has two parts. The helper verb haben is part 2. The past participle, for example gespielt, waits at the very end. It is the same shape as kann ... spielen from chapter 5.
cards.more: A bracket has two sides, and everything else sits between them. In the modal bracket the left side is kann and the right side is the infinitive spielen. In the Perfekt the left side is habe and the right side is the participle gespielt. Left side: always the second part of the sentence. Right side: always the very last word. If you remember where the two sides go, the middle can hold anything, such as Tennis or Fußball.
cards.lead: In the last card you saw war and the new Perfekt. On this card: the shape of the Perfekt, which matches the modal bracket you already know, so a new rule feels familiar.

deeper.text: A bracket also helps in longer sentences. The more words you put in the middle, the more important the ending becomes. Always read to the end of the German sentence: the participle often holds the main action, like gespielt or gemacht.

cards.title: haben: all six forms
cards.body: The helper verb is haben, which you know from chapter 2. It changes with the person: ich habe, du hast, er/sie hat, wir haben, ihr habt, sie/Sie haben. In the Perfekt it always takes part 2.
cards.more: You already know haben as the verb for having things: Ich habe Hunger. In the Perfekt it does a second job: it is a helper that stands in the second place. Only the helper changes with the person. The participle at the end never changes: gespielt stays gespielt for ich, du, er and all the others. So you only need to learn each participle once. Look at the table and read each row aloud.
cards.lead: Last card you saw the bracket, with habe on the left. On this card: all six forms of haben, so you can say what you, he, she or they did.

deeper.text: Notice the little changes: hast ends in -st, hat has no ending, habt ends in -t. Only wir and sie/Sie keep the full form haben. If you mix up hat and habt, check the person first: one person (er, sie, Leon) is hat, several people you talk to (ihr) is habt.

cards.title: Find the participle in 3 steps
cards.body: A regular participle is easy to make. Take the infinitive, cut off -en to get the stem, then add ge- in front and -t at the end: spielen, spiel, gespielt. The ten verbs in the table all work this way.
steps: Take the infinitive: spielen
Cut off -en: spiel
Add ge- in front and -t at the end: ge + spiel + t = gespielt
cards.more: Making a participle is like putting a sandwich together. The stem is the filling: spiel. Ge- is the bread on the left, and -t is the bread on the right. So ge + spiel + t gives gespielt. Do the three steps for every new verb: infinitive, stem, then bread on both sides. Verbs like machen, lernen and kochen all follow this recipe, and so do the other seven in the table.
cards.lead: You know the helper verb now. On this card: how to make the participle in three small steps, so you can use ten everyday verbs in the Perfekt.

deeper.text: Some participles look just like the present form of er/sie: er macht and gemacht share the same stem. The difference is the ge- at the start. If a word starts with ge- and ends in -t, it is very likely a regular participle. This small trick helps when you read a text.

cards.title: Say it: Ich habe gestern ...
cards.body: Add a time word to say when: gestern, vorgestern, letzte Woche, letztes Wochenende. It can stand in the middle or at the front. If the time comes first, haben is still part 2, and the participle is still last.

examples.en: The day before yesterday I played football.

examples.why: time first: habe is still part 2.

examples.de: Letzte Woche hat Mira Kaffee gekocht.

cards.more: A time word is like a flag you plant. It says when. You can plant it right after the helper verb, or at the very front of the sentence. In both cases, the helper verb stays in the second place. At the front, the subject jumps behind the verb: Gestern habe ich. That is the same trick as in earlier chapters. The participle never moves from the end. Try the three rows of the table, one after the other.
cards.lead: Now you can build a Perfekt sentence. On this card: the time words for yesterday and last week, and where they fit, so you can say when something happened.

deeper.text: The little words schon and noch nicht are useful too. Ich habe schon gelernt means I have already learned. Ich habe noch nicht gekocht means I have not cooked yet. For now, learn noch nicht as one chunk. You will use it fully in a later lesson.

cards.title: Ask: Was hast du gemacht?
cards.body: Ask what happened with a W-question: Was hast du gemacht? The verb haben is part 2, the participle is last. A yes/no question starts with haben: Hast du Tennis gespielt? Use haben with Sie: Was haben Sie gemacht?
cards.more: Questions in the Perfekt follow the rules you already know. In a W-question the helper verb is part 2, right after was. In a yes/no question the helper verb moves to the very front. In both cases the participle still waits at the end, like the last piece of a puzzle. For a friend you say hast du, for a polite person you say haben Sie. A short answer starts with Ja, ich habe, and then you add the participle.
cards.lead: You can now say what you did. On this card: how to ask a friend or a polite person what they did, so you can start a talk about yesterday.

deeper.text: A short answer often drops the participle you already heard. Hast du Tennis gespielt? Ja, habe ich. is natural in speech. As a beginner, say the full sentence: Ja, ich habe Tennis gespielt. It is longer but always correct, and it trains the bracket.

cards.title: A study day
cards.body: Now put it to work at the Uni. Use the new words Vorlesung, Prüfung, Fach and Semester with the Perfekt. Ich habe in der Vorlesung gefragt. Ich habe für die Prüfung geübt. The participle stays last, even after a longer phrase.

examples.why: in der Vorlesung is the middle.

examples.de: Ich habe für die Prüfung geübt.
examples.why: für die Prüfung is the middle.

examples.de: Mira hat im Semester viel gelernt.
examples.en: Mira learned a lot in the semester.
examples.why: viel is part of the middle.

cards.more: At the Uni, you often tell friends what you did: you asked a question, you practised, you learned a lot. With the Perfekt you can do that already. The middle of the bracket can be long: in der Vorlesung, für die Prüfung, viel. The two sides stay the same. Left side: habe or hat. Right side: the participle. Try to say each example aloud twice, and then change the verb: gefragt, geübt, gelernt.
cards.lead: You have all the pieces now. On this card, the last of the lesson: the Uni words Vorlesung, Prüfung, Fach and Semester in real Perfekt sentences, so you can talk about a study day.

deeper.text: Words like Prüfung and Vorlesung are feminine, so they take die and eine. After für you use die Prüfung. In der Vorlesung is a place phrase, and der shows the word is feminine. You only need to copy these phrases as they are for now.

example.de: Wir haben für das Fach viel gelernt.
example.en: We learned a lot for the subject.

lessons.title: arbeiten gearbeitet: the extra e, and how is your job?
lessons.goal: Make participles with the extra e (gearbeitet) and say how your job is.

grammar.point: If the verb stem ends in -t, -d, -gn, -fn or -chn, the participle is ge + stem + et: gearbeitet.
grammar.oneLine: Ich habe gestern gearbeitet. Es hat geregnet.

mistake.why: The stem arbeit ends in -t, so you need an extra e before the final -t.

terms.meaning: an e added to help you say the word: gearbeitet
the verb without -en: arbeit

cards.title: Before we start: how was work?
cards.body: A friend asks: How was work? You want to say: I worked, I waited, it rained. Some verbs need an extra e, and you already know that from the present: du arbeitest, er arbeitet. The same verbs take the extra e in the Perfekt.

examples.why: You know this already: arbeitest has an extra e.
New today: ge + stem + et = gearbeitet.

steps: You already know: du arbeitest, er wartet: the extra e in the present (chapter 2), and ge...t from lesson 1
New today: some participles are ge + stem + et, e.g. gearbeitet
By the end you can: say what you did at work and say how your job is
cards.more: Say arbeitet aloud, then say arbeitt. The second one is impossible to pronounce: two t sounds crash into each other. German puts an e in the middle to help your mouth. That is the extra e. It is not a new rule: you did the same in the present, du arbeitest and er arbeitet. Now it moves into the participle: gearbeitet. In the next cards you learn which verbs need it and how to spot them.

cards.title: Remember the extra e
cards.body: In the present, arbeiten needs an extra e: du arbeitest, er arbeitet. Spielen does not: du spielst, er spielt. Verbs with the extra e in the present have it in the Perfekt too: gearbeitet, but gespielt.
cards.more: A mouth-saver is what the extra e really is. After a t or a d, adding another -t is hard to say, so German adds a small e in between. You already did this in chapter 2 with arbeiten and warten. Now check the table: the extra e in du arbeitest and er arbeitet is the same e you see in gearbeitet. For spielen there is no problem for your mouth, so no extra e: spielt, gespielt.
cards.lead: In lesson 1 you made participles like gespielt. On this card: you see that the extra e from the present comes back in the Perfekt, so a form like gearbeitet will not surprise you.

deeper.text: Pronounce the difference: gespielt has one clean t at the end. Gearbeitet has an extra syllable, so it has four parts: ge-ar-bei-tet. If you say it slowly, your mouth shows you where the e belongs. Say it three times and listen for the extra beat before the final t.

cards.title: ge + stem + et
cards.body: Add an extra e: ge + stem + et. Arbeiten: stem arbeit, so gearbeitet. Warten: gewartet. The helper is still haben in part 2 and the participle is still last. Kosten also follows it: gekostet.

examples.de: Das Brot hat zwei Euro gekostet.

cards.more: The recipe has one change from lesson 1. Before it was ge + stem + t: gespielt. Now it is ge + stem + et: gearbeitet. The e is the small bridge between the stem and the final t. Everything else stays the same: haben in the second place, the participle at the end. Learn the eight verbs in the table by reading them aloud once. They are common at work and at home.
cards.lead: You know that the extra e exists. On this card: the recipe ge + stem + et and eight verbs that use it, so you can talk about work and waiting.

deeper.text: Antworten and zeichnen are good to remember because they look different in the present: er antwortet, er zeichnet. The extra e is hard to hear in fast speech, but you must write it. A good habit is to check the end of the stem: is it t, d, or something hard to say?

cards.title: When do you add the extra e?
cards.body: Look at the stem, the verb without -en. Add the extra e if the stem ends in -t or -d, or in -gn, -fn or -chn. Do not add it after -l, -r or -h: lernen is gelernt, wohnen is gewohnt.

examples.why: wart ends in t: extra e.
lern ends in rn: no extra e.
bad ends in d: extra e.

steps: Cut off -en: warten, wart
Look at the end of the stem: t, d, gn, fn or chn?
Yes: add the extra e: ge + wart + et = gewartet. No: ge + stem + t.
cards.more: Do three quick checks for any new verb. First cut off -en. Second look at the last letters of the stem. Third decide: t or d at the end, or gn, fn, chn? Then add the extra e. Does the stem end in l, r or h before the n? Then no extra e, because your mouth has no problem there. Practise with spielen, which has no extra e, and then with warten and regnen, which both need it.
cards.lead: You have seen eight verbs with the extra e. On this card: a simple test so you can decide for every new verb whether it needs the extra e or not.

deeper.text: Sometimes you can simply listen: if the stem ends in a hard sound like t, d, or a group like -chn, an extra syllable is needed to say the word. If your mouth can say the stem + t easily, as in spiel + t, then no e is needed.

cards.title: Es hat geregnet
cards.body: Weather verbs have the subject es. Es regnet means it rains. In the Perfekt the helper is hat, because es goes with hat: Es hat gestern geregnet. Never habe: only ich takes habe.
cards.more: It is like English: it rained. The word es stands for nobody in particular, it is just the weather. Because es is er/sie/es, the helper is hat, like in Leon hat or Mira hat. The participle geregnet comes from regnen: the stem regn ends in -gn, so you need the extra e. Say Es hat geregnet three times, and then say it with Montag at the front.
cards.lead: You have the rule for the extra e. On this card: the weather verb regnen and its helper hat, so you can say that it rained.

deeper.text: You can also say that it did not rain: Es hat nicht geregnet. Notice that nicht stands before the participle, in the middle of the bracket. You will practise this more later. For now, remember: es hat geregnet, and es hat nicht geregnet.

cards.title: Describe your job
cards.body: Say how your job is with chunks. Der Job macht Spaß. Die Arbeit ist anstrengend. Der Job ist gut bezahlt or schlecht bezahlt. Learn gut bezahlt and schlecht bezahlt as whole chunks for now. Spaß machen also works in the Perfekt.
cards.more: Think of these as little phrases you can use like building blocks. Der Job macht Spaß means the job gives joy. Die Arbeit ist anstrengend means the work is tiring. Gut bezahlt and schlecht bezahlt tell you about the money: well paid or badly paid. You do not need to take bezahlt apart today. Just learn it as a whole. Lesson 3 explains it. To talk about the past: Der Job hat Spaß gemacht.
cards.lead: You can say what you did at work. On this card: short phrases for how a job is, such as fun, tiring or well paid, so you can answer How is your job?

deeper.text: Chunks are the fastest way to speak. You do not build them, you remember them whole: gut bezahlt, schlecht bezahlt, Spaß machen. In the past, only the helper changes: macht Spaß becomes hat Spaß gemacht. The old Spaß stays in the middle of the bracket.

cards.title: Overtime and a Praktikum
cards.body: Two new job words with machen: Überstunden machen means to work overtime, ein Praktikum machen means to do an internship. Both use gemacht from lesson 1. Überstunde is a die-word, plural Überstunden. Praktikum is a das-word, plural Praktika.

examples.en: I worked two hours of overtime.

examples.de: Frau Weber hat gestern Überstunden gemacht.

cards.more: Germans say they make overtime and make an internship, just like English make a call. So the verb stays the same easy one: machen, and the participle is gemacht, which you already know. The new part is the two nouns. Überstunden is a plural word, so there is no ein before it. Praktikum is a das-word, so ein Praktikum. Salary is das Gehalt, and a position or job is die Stelle.
cards.lead: You can describe a job. On this card: Überstunden and Praktikum with the verb machen, so you can say what extra work you did.

deeper.text: A Praktikum is a short job to learn about a company, often during or after your studies. The plural is unusual: die Praktika, not Praktikums. It comes from Latin. You do not need to guess the plural: learn it with the word.

cards.title: Review: ge...t or ge...et?
cards.body: Sort the participles. Most verbs are ge + stem + t, like gespielt, gemacht, gelernt. Verbs with a stem ending in t, d, gn, fn or chn need the extra e: gearbeitet, gewartet, geregnet. Check the stem each time.
cards.more: Sorting helps your brain more than reading a list. Look at the two columns. In the left column the stem is easy to say, so only t is added. In the right column the stem ends in a hard spot, so an extra e is added to help you. When you meet a new verb, do the three-step test from the card When do you add the extra e?: cut off -en, check the end of the stem, then decide. This quick check will soon feel automatic.
cards.lead: You have seen both kinds of participle. On this card, the last of the lesson: a short sorting so you can decide between ge...t and ge...et quickly.

deeper.text: If you are not sure, say the stem and add -t aloud. Is it easy to say? Then no extra e. Is it hard, as in arbeit + t? Then add the e. The sound often tells you the answer, and the spelling follows. Check the table when you write.

lessons.title: studieren, telefonieren: verbs without ge-
lessons.goal: Make participles without ge- (studiert, bezahlt) and talk about your studies and your job.

grammar.point: Verbs ending in -ieren and verbs starting with be-, ver- or er- have no ge-: stem + t (studiert, bezahlt).
grammar.oneLine: Ich habe Informatik studiert. Ich habe Pizza bestellt.

mistake.why: Verbs that end in -ieren have no ge-. You only add -t to the stem.

terms.meaning: a verb ending in -ieren, like studieren; its participle has no ge-
the beginning be- or ver- that is glued to a verb

cards.title: Before we start: what did you study, what do you do?
cards.body: Someone asks: What did you study? What is your job? Most participles start with ge-, but some do not. Verbs like studieren and telefonieren have no ge-, and neither do verbs that start with be- or ver-. You know telefonieren already.

examples.why: New today: telefoniert has no ge-.

steps: You already know: ge...t from gespielt and ge...et from gearbeitet (lessons 1 and 2), and telefonieren (chapter 5)
New today: participles without ge-: telefoniert, studiert, bezahlt
By the end you can: say what you studied and what you did at work, with job words
cards.more: Try to say getelefoniert. It sounds clumsy, doesn't it? German has a simple trick: if a verb already has a clear beginning or a stressed -ie- sound, it needs no ge- in front. That is why telefoniert and studiert look short. In the next cards you will see two groups of verbs without ge-: the -ieren verbs, and the verbs that start with be- or ver-. You will also learn four jobs and how to say what you do.

cards.title: The ge- is not always there
cards.body: Most participles have ge- in front: gespielt, gelernt, gearbeitet. A few groups do not. Compare gespielt with telefoniert. You learn the two groups on the next cards: -ieren verbs and verbs that start with be- or ver-.
cards.more: Compare the two kinds of participle like two kinds of bread: one has a crust on the front, which is ge-, and one has not. Both are fine to eat, you just need to know which is which. The next two cards give you two easy signs. Sign one: the verb ends in -ieren. Sign two: the verb starts with be- or ver-. If you see one of those signs, do not add ge-.
cards.lead: In lessons 1 and 2 every participle had ge-. On this card: you see that some do not, so the next two cards make sense.

deeper.text: A good rule is this: the ge- goes in front of the stressed part of the verb. In spielen the stress is on spie-, so ge-spielt. In studieren the stress is on -die-, which is in the middle, so there is no room for ge- in front. You do not need to remember this now, but it helps when you listen.

cards.title: -ieren verbs: no ge-
cards.body: Verbs that end in -ieren have no ge-. Take the stem and add t: studieren, studiert. The stress is on -ie-. You know telefonieren and probieren. Reparieren, organisieren and fotografieren follow the same rule.

examples.en: Ben took a photo of Mira.

steps: Infinitive: studieren
Cut off -en: studier
Add only -t, no ge-: studiert
cards.more: The rule is shorter than the one for ge...t: for -ieren verbs you only add -t. No ge-, no extra e. Take studieren: remove -en, you have studier, add t, and you have studiert. Say the word and hear the stress on -die-: stu-DIE-ren. That stress is the sign that a verb has no ge-. There are many -ieren verbs in German, and many of them look like English: organise, photograph, repair, study.
cards.lead: You know that some participles have no ge-. On this card: the first group, the -ieren verbs, so you can say studiert, repariert or organisiert.

deeper.text: Many -ieren verbs come from Latin or French, so they often look like English words: studieren is study, reparieren is repair. When you see a new German verb that ends in -ieren, you can already guess the participle: stem + t, no ge-.

cards.title: Also no ge-: be-, ver-, er-
cards.body: Verbs that start with be-, ver- or er- have no ge- either. The beginning already does the job. Bezahlen is bezahlt, so gut bezahlt means well paid, as in lesson 2. Besuchen is besucht, bestellen is bestellt, verdienen is verdient, erklären (to explain) is erklärt.
cards.more: In lesson 2 you learned gut bezahlt as a chunk. Now you can see what is inside: bezahlt is the participle of bezahlen. The job is paid well. The sign is the beginning: be- at the start of bezahlen, besuchen and bestellen, ver- at the start of verdienen. These beginnings are small words that are glued to the verb. So there is no room for ge-. The rest is easy: stem + t, like in lesson 1.
cards.lead: You know the -ieren group. On this card: the second group, verbs that start with be- or ver-, so you can say bezahlt, besucht, bestellt and verdient.

deeper.text: Look at the beginning of the verb, not at the end. Be- and ver- are not words on their own, but they change the meaning: zahlen is to pay, bezahlen is to pay for. The stem of bestellen ends in -ll, not in t or d, so it needs no extra e: bestellt, not bestellet.

cards.title: What did you study? What do you do?
cards.body: Say what you studied with studiert: Ich habe Informatik studiert. Say your job with arbeiten als, and no article: Ich arbeite als Programmierer. A woman adds -in: Programmiererin. Jobs here: Ingenieur, Mechaniker, Pfleger, Programmierer.

examples.en: My sister works as a nurse.

cards.more: Two questions come up again and again: What did you study? and What do you do? For the first you use the Perfekt: Ich habe Informatik studiert. For the second you use the present: Ich arbeite als Programmierer. The word als means as, and it comes before the job. There is no article before a job. For women, add -in at the end, as in chapter 1. In the table you see four jobs, with the woman's form and the plural.
cards.lead: You have two groups of participles without ge-. On this card: how to say what you studied and what your job is, so you can talk about your life.

deeper.text: To talk about a job, the easiest way is to say your own: Ich arbeite als Mechaniker. Remember two things. First, there is no ein before the job. Second, a woman adds -in: Mechanikerin. If you forget the -in, people still understand you, but the correct form sounds much more natural.

cards.title: What does a mechanic do?
cards.body: Now join jobs and participles. A mechanic repairs: Der Mechaniker hat das Auto repariert. A nurse phones: Die Pflegerin hat viel telefoniert. An engineer organises: Der Ingenieur hat das Projekt organisiert.

cards.more: A job sentence in the Perfekt is just like the sentences you know. The subject can be a job: der Mechaniker, die Pflegerin, der Ingenieur. After it comes hat in the second place. The objects like das Auto or das Projekt sit in the middle. The participle is last, and it has no ge-. Try changing the job in each sentence: Die Ingenieurin hat das Auto repariert. It is a good way to practise the bracket.
cards.lead: You know the jobs and the participles. On this card: sentences about what a mechanic, a nurse and an engineer did, so you can talk about work in the Perfekt.

deeper.text: The subject can be a man or a woman: der Mechaniker or die Mechanikerin. The helper is hat for both, because each is one person. Only the article and the -in change. The participle stays the same, repariert, for everyone.

example.de: Die Mechanikerin hat das Auto repariert.

cards.title: Review: ge...t, ge...et or no ge-?
cards.body: Sort the participles into three groups. Most are ge + stem + t: gespielt. After a hard stem add an extra e: gearbeitet. With -ieren verbs and be-/ver- verbs, add no ge-: studiert, bezahlt. Check the verb each time.
cards.more: Three small questions solve every regular participle. Question one: does the verb end in -ieren or start with be- or ver-? Then no ge-, just stem + t. Question two: does the stem end in t, d, gn, fn or chn? Then ge + stem + et. Question three: everything else is ge + stem + t. Try the table and say a sentence for each row. After a few rounds you will do this without thinking.
cards.lead: You have all three kinds of regular participle. On this card, the last of the lesson: a three-way sorting, so you can choose the right form for any verb.

deeper.text: If you are ever unsure, check a dictionary. It shows the forms: besuchen, besucht, hat besucht. Look for the little bracket after each verb in the word list of your dictionary: it tells you the participle and also whether the helper is haben or sein. Make a habit of copying the participle together with every new verb.

lessons.title: Irregular participles: gegessen, getrunken, gesehen
lessons.goal: Use the common irregular participles with haben and say where people work.

grammar.point: Irregular verbs make the participle as ge + stem (often changed) + en. Learn the three forms together: essen - isst - gegessen.
grammar.oneLine: Ich habe Pizza gegessen. Helper verb in part 2, participle at the end.

mistake.why: essen is irregular, so the participle is gegessen, not ge + stem + t.

terms.meaning: a verb whose participle you learn by heart because it does not follow ge + stem + t
the verb form at the very end of the Perfekt, for example gegessen
haben in part 2 of the sentence; it works together with the participle

cards.title: Before we start: what did you eat, see, read?
cards.body: A real moment: a friend asks, Was hast du gestern gegessen? In lesson 1 you learned ge + stem + t, as in gespielt. Some very common verbs, like essen and trinken, use a different ending. Today you learn them, and the places where people work.
steps: You already know: Ich habe Tennis gespielt, the Perfekt from lesson 1.
New today: verbs that end in -en, like gegessen and getrunken.
By the end you can: say Ich habe Pizza gegessen und Tee getrunken.

examples.why: You know this: haben + ge + stem + t, from lesson 1.
New today: essen does not give geesst. It gives gegessen.

cards.more: Think of the Perfekt as a box with two ends. The helper verb sits in the second spot, and the participle waits at the very end. In lesson 1 the participle was easy to build: ge, then the stem, then t. Now meet verbs that built their participle in a different way, a long time ago. They end in -en, and the middle often changes. You learn each one as a small set of three, like essen, isst, gegessen. You will do this step by step, with a table, two small groups and plenty of examples.

cards.title: Some verbs do not follow ge-stem-t
cards.body: Most verbs follow ge + stem + t. A small group do not. They end in -en: ge + stem + en, and the stem often changes. You learn each one as a set of three forms: essen, isst, gegessen.

examples.why: Irregular: learn gegessen as one whole word.

cards.more: Regular verbs are like a recipe you can repeat: ge, stem, t. Irregular verbs are like family recipes where the cook changed one ingredient. You cannot guess them, so you remember each one. Step 1: see essen. Step 2: do not say geesst. Step 3: say gegessen from memory. Good news: the eleven you need most are in the next card, and you already know the present forms from earlier chapters.
cards.lead: In lesson 1 you built gespielt from spiel. Now meet verbs that break that recipe: essen gives gegessen, not geesst. On this card you see the new ending -en.

deeper.text: English does the same. Play becomes played, which is regular, but eat becomes eaten and drink becomes drunk, which are not. Many German irregular participles even look like their English cousins: getrunken and drunk, gesehen and seen. Use that link to help you remember them.

cards.title: ge ... en: the pattern
cards.body: Learn the three forms together. The participle starts with ge and ends in -en. The middle is the stem, and it often changes: trinken becomes getrunken. These eleven come first. A table like this is your cheat sheet.
cards.more: Imagine eleven friends, and each one has three names: one for now, one for he or she, and one for yesterday. Essen, isst, gegessen. You say all three out loud, like a little song. Step 1: cover the English. Step 2: say the infinitive. Step 3: say the participle. Do this once a day and it sticks fast. Extra example: Ich habe Wasser getrunken means I drank water.
cards.lead: You saw that essen gives gegessen. On this card you meet eleven useful verbs in one table, so you can talk about what you ate, drank, saw, read and wrote.

deeper.text: Look at the table again. The participle keeps -en at the end, but the stem vowel can change, like i to u in trinken or e to o in sprechen. Also nehmen doubles the m (genommen) and treffen keeps ff. Spell them with care: one wrong letter looks odd to a German reader.

cards.title: Learn them in sets
cards.body: Group 1: the vowel stays the same (gegessen, gelesen, gesehen, geschlafen, gegeben). Group 2: the vowel changes (getrunken, geschrieben, gesprochen, genommen, getroffen, gefunden). Say each group out loud. Short lists stick better.
cards.more: Think of sorting socks. If you throw all of them into one drawer, you search for ages. If you make two piles, you find a pair at once. Pile 1 is the same-vowel pile: the middle sound does not move. Pile 2 is the changing pile: the middle sound jumps, like trinken to getrunken. Step 1: read pile 1 aloud. Step 2: read pile 2 aloud. Step 3: cover the table and try to say one from each pile.
cards.lead: You have all eleven in one table. Next we sort them into two small groups, because a short group is easier to remember than eleven loose words.

deeper.text: Careful: a vowel change in the present does not mean the same change in the participle. Er liest has ie, but the participle is gelesen with a plain e. Er sieht has ie, but the participle is gesehen. Learn the participle on its own, as its own word.

example.de: Sie liest heute und hat gestern eine Zeitung gelesen.
example.en: She reads today and read a newspaper yesterday.

cards.title: A meal and a day
cards.body: A short sentence can share one helper verb: habe covers both parts. Each participle ends its own part: Ich habe Pizza gegessen und Tee getrunken. The time word can go first, but the helper verb stays in part 2.

examples.de: Ich habe Pizza gegessen und Tee getrunken.
examples.en: I ate pizza and drank tea.
examples.why: One helper verb, two participles, joined by und.

examples.de: Gestern haben wir einen Film gesehen.
examples.why: Time first, helper verb still part 2.
Question word first, helper verb part 2.

cards.more: Picture two train carriages pulled by one engine. The engine is habe, and it pulls both carriages: the pizza carriage and the tea carriage. Each carriage ends with its own participle. If you start with gestern, the engine does not move: it stays in the second place, and ich hops behind it. Step 1: choose the engine. Step 2: add the first thing and its participle. Step 3: add und and the second thing and its participle.
cards.lead: Now you can put the verbs to work. On this card: one helper verb that serves two participles joined by und, so you can tell what you ate and drank in a single sentence.

deeper.text: In everyday talk Germans use the Perfekt a lot for the past. When a friend asks Was hast du gestern gemacht?, you can answer with any verb from this lesson. Short answers are fine too, because the helper verb is clear from the question. Learn to say a full sentence first, then shorten it.

example.de: Heute Morgen habe ich Brot gegessen.

cards.title: Reading, writing, speaking at work
cards.body: At work you read, write and speak a lot, and the same bracket works: Ich habe eine E-Mail geschrieben. With sprechen, add mit and the person: Wir haben mit dem Chef gesprochen. Learn mit dem Chef as one piece.

examples.de: Wir haben mit dem Chef gesprochen.
Meine Schwester hat eine Stelle gefunden.

cards.more: At work, most of the day is little tasks: read this, write that, talk to someone, meet someone. Each task is one verb from your table. Step 1: pick the task. Step 2: pick the verb. Step 3: put habe or hat in the second place and the participle last. Extra example: Ich habe die Kollegin getroffen means I met the colleague. With sprechen, do not forget mit: you speak with someone.
cards.lead: You can already talk about food. Next you meet work: the same verbs for mail, letters and meetings. On this card you also see that sprechen needs mit and treffen does not.

deeper.text: Treffen takes the person directly: Ich habe Anna getroffen. Sprechen needs mit: Ich habe mit Anna gesprochen. English does the same when you say talk with someone. If you forget mit, the sentence sounds wrong. A quick check: after sprechen ask with whom? and add mit; after treffen no extra word is needed.

cards.title: Where did you work? Workplaces
cards.body: Learn the place with its word for where. Use in for most places: in der Fabrik, in der Werkstatt, im Geschäft. Two are special: auf der Baustelle and am Arbeitsplatz. Learn each one as one piece. You know in der and im from chapters 7 and 9.

examples.en: My uncle worked in the workshop.

examples.de: Frau Weber hat im Geschäft Brot gekauft.
examples.en: Frau Weber bought bread in the shop.

examples.de: Der Handwerker hat auf der Baustelle gearbeitet.
examples.en: The craftsman worked on the building site.
examples.why: auf der Baustelle: another piece to learn.

cards.more: Think of each work place as a label with its own small sticker for where. Fabrik gets in der, Werkstatt gets in der, Geschäft gets im, Baustelle gets auf der, Arbeitsplatz gets am. You do not need to ask why yet. Step 1: learn the place. Step 2: learn the sticker with it. Step 3: put the whole block in the middle of the sentence. Extra example: Ich habe am Arbeitsplatz Kaffee getrunken. A craftsperson is der Handwerker, and a woman is die Handwerkerin.
cards.lead: So far the sentences were about food and mail. On this card: five words for places where people work, and in + the place, so you can say where you worked.

deeper.text: Draußen and drinnen are small words that say outside and inside. They need no in and no ending. Craftspeople often work draußen, and office workers often work drinnen. Put them in the middle, just like a place block: after the helper verb and the subject, and before the participle.

cards.title: Review: ge...t or ge...en?
cards.body: Ask one question: is this verb one of the irregular verbs from the table? Yes: learn ge + ... + en. No: use ge + stem + t. Verbs with an extra e (gearbeitet) or without ge (studiert) have their own rules from lessons 2 and 3.

examples.why: Irregular: on the table, so ge...en.
Regular: not on the table, so ge...t.

examples.de: Ben hat Kuchen gekauft und gegessen.
examples.en: Ben bought cake and ate it.
examples.why: Regular and irregular in one sentence.

steps: Look at the verb: is it on the irregular list?
Yes: use the learned participle (gegessen, getrunken, gesehen ...).
No: use ge + stem + t, with an extra e or without ge when needed.
cards.more: Think of two doors. Door 1 says ge, stem, t. Door 2 says ge, stem, en. Before you go in, check your cheat sheet. If the verb is on the list, take door 2. If it is not, take door 1, but check the extra e and the no-ge cases. Step 1: look at the verb. Step 2: check the list. Step 3: choose the door. Your ear will learn the sound after a while.
cards.lead: Now you know two recipes: ge + stem + t and ge + stem + en. On this last card you practise choosing the right one and mixing everything from lessons 1 to 4.

deeper.text: Whenever you are unsure, say the three forms in your head. If the verb is on your table, you know the answer. If not, build it with ge + stem + t. When a regular verb has an extra e, say it aloud: gearbeitet sounds better than gearbeitt. Your ear helps you.

example.en: Mira studied computer science and read books.

lessons.title: sein with movement: ich bin gefahren, gegangen, geflogen
lessons.goal: Say where you went and how, using sein with the first movement verbs.

grammar.point: Verbs of movement from A to B use sein as the helper verb: ich bin, du bist, er/sie ist, wir sind, ihr seid, sie/Sie sind + participle.
grammar.oneLine: Ich bin nach Berlin gefahren. Sein in part 2, participle at the end.

mistake.why: fahren is a movement from A to B, so the helper verb is sein.

terms.meaning: a verb that takes you from one place to another, like fahren or gehen
the second helper verb: it goes with movement verbs in the Perfekt
on foot; learn it as one piece

cards.title: Before we start: how did you get there?
cards.body: A real moment: a colleague asks, Wie bist du zur Arbeit gekommen? So far your Perfekt used haben. Some verbs need a different helper verb: sein. Today you learn which verbs those are, and how to say how you travelled and where to.
steps: You already know: Ich fahre mit dem Bus, from chapters 3 and 7.
New today: sein as the helper verb for movement, as in Ich bin gefahren.
By the end you can: say Ich bin mit dem Bus zur Arbeit gefahren.

examples.de: Ich fahre mit dem Bus zur Arbeit.
examples.en: I go to work by bus.
examples.why: You know this: fahren + mit dem Bus.

examples.de: Ich bin mit dem Bus zur Arbeit gefahren.
examples.en: I went to work by bus.

cards.more: Think of two bus drivers. Driver Haben takes care of everyday jobs: eating, reading, working. Driver Sein takes care of trips, when you go from one place to another. The bracket is the same for both: the helper verb in the second spot and the participle at the end. Only the driver changes. You will meet the drivers one at a time: the forms of sein, the six movement verbs, how to say how you travelled, and a simple test to pick the right driver.

cards.title: Two helper verbs
cards.body: Most verbs take haben: you do something. Verbs of movement from A to B take sein: you go somewhere. The bracket stays the same, only the helper changes: Ich habe gegessen, but Ich bin gefahren.

examples.why: Going from A to B: sein.
Going from A to B: sein.

headers: sein (you go from A to B)

cards.more: Ask yourself one thing: did I leave one place and arrive in another? If yes, call driver Sein. If you only did something where you were, call driver Haben. Eating pizza does not move you, so haben. Driving to Berlin moves you, so sein. Step 1: spot the verb. Step 2: ask did I move. Step 3: choose the helper. The participle ending does not change the choice.
cards.lead: In lesson 4 every sentence used haben. On this card you meet the second helper verb, sein, and the one question that picks between the two.

deeper.text: Most verbs use haben, and only a short list uses sein, so haben is your safe default. The sein list is mostly movement: fahren, gehen, kommen, fliegen. You will learn the full test in a few cards, and in lesson 6 you add one more group.

cards.title: sein: bin, bist, ist, sind, seid, sind
cards.body: The forms of sein are the ones you already know: ich bin, du bist, er/sie ist, wir sind, ihr seid, sie/Sie sind. As a helper verb it sits in part 2, and the participle goes last, just like with haben.

examples.de: Wir sind mit dem Zug gefahren.

cards.more: You already own this toolbox: ich bin, du bist and the rest. Now the tool has a second job. Before it said who you are. Now it holds a bracket together. Step 1: pick the right form for the person. Step 2: put it in the second spot. Step 3: finish with the participle. Say all six aloud: ich bin gefahren, du bist gefahren, er ist gefahren, wir sind gefahren, ihr seid gefahren, sie sind gefahren.
cards.lead: You know ich bin and du bist from chapter 2. On this card the same forms become helper verbs, with the participle waiting at the end.

deeper.text: Two forms look alike: sie ist means she is, and sie sind means they are. In the Perfekt it works the same: Sie ist gefahren means she went, and Sie sind gefahren means they went. Look at the helper verb to know who is meant. Sie sind with a capital S can also mean you, the polite form.

cards.title: The movement verbs
cards.body: These six verbs all show movement from A to B, so they take sein. Five are irregular (ge...en). Reisen is regular (gereist) but still takes sein. Learn the six as one set.

examples.de: Mira ist letztes Jahr nach Wien gereist.
examples.en: Mira travelled to Vienna last year.

cards.more: These six verbs are the travelling verbs, the ones with suitcases. Fahren, gehen, kommen, fliegen, laufen and reisen all get you from here to there. Because the person moves, they pick driver Sein. Five of them have the -en participle you know from lesson 4. Reisen is the rebel: its participle is regular, gereist, but it still takes sein. Step 1: read the table. Step 2: say the three forms. Step 3: cover and repeat.
cards.lead: You can build the bracket with sein. On this card you meet the six verbs that take it first, so you can say where you went, drove, flew or came.

deeper.text: Reisen proves the rule: it is regular, so its participle is gereist, but it still takes sein, because you travel from A to B. The helper verb depends on the meaning, which is movement, not on whether the participle is regular. Remember this when you meet new verbs.

example.de: Herr Ali ist nach Hamburg gereist.

cards.title: How did you get to work? mit dem + vehicle
cards.body: To say how you travelled, put mit dem and the vehicle in the middle: Ich bin mit dem Bus gefahren. On foot is zu Fuß: Wir sind zu Fuß gegangen. Learn mit dem + vehicle as one piece. For die-words it is mit der.

examples.de: Ich bin mit dem Bus zur Arbeit gefahren.
examples.en: I went to work by bus.

examples.de: Mira ist mit dem Zug gekommen.

cards.more: Think of mit dem as a small ticket. You show the ticket and name the vehicle: mit dem Bus, mit dem Zug, mit dem Auto, mit dem Fahrrad. Die-words print a different ticket: mit der Straßenbahn. Walking needs no ticket at all: zu Fuß, which means on foot. Step 1: choose the vehicle. Step 2: add its ticket. Step 3: put the block in the middle, before the participle.
cards.lead: You can say that you went. Next: how you went. On this card you learn mit dem and the vehicle, and zu Fuß for on foot.

deeper.text: In English you can go on the bus, but in German you go mit dem Bus, which is with the bus. For a bicycle it is mit dem Fahrrad, not on the bicycle. A Wie-question asks for this block: Wie bist du gekommen? Mit dem Zug, or zu Fuß.

example.de: Ben ist mit dem Fahrrad gefahren.

cards.title: Where from, where to: aus, von, zu, nach
cards.body: Four small words give the direction. Aus and von say from where. Zu and nach say to where. Use nach with cities and with nach Hause. Use zu with most other places. Learn each block as one piece: aus dem Büro, zum Bahnhof.

examples.de: Ich bin aus dem Büro gekommen.
examples.en: I came out of the office.

rows: coming from a place or person
going to a city or home

cards.more: Imagine a street with two signs. One arrow points away and says aus or von: where you left. One arrow points ahead and says zu or nach: where you are heading. Cities and home get nach. Most other places get zu. Step 1: decide from or to. Step 2: pick the small word. Step 3: add the place as one block. Extra example: Anna ist zur Arbeit gegangen means Anna went to work.
cards.lead: You can say how you travelled. Now you add where from and where to, with four small words: aus, von, zu and nach.

deeper.text: Aus and von both mean from. Aus is for coming out of an inside place, like aus dem Büro or aus der Werkstatt. Von is for coming from a place you were near, or from a person: von der Uni. If you are unsure, use aus for rooms and buildings you were inside, and von for the rest.

example.de: Mira ist von der Uni nach Hause gelaufen.

cards.title: haben or sein? The 3-step test
cards.body: Use this test each time you build a Perfekt. Compare: Ich habe gearbeitet, no new place. Ich bin gefahren, a new place. The test looks at the meaning, not at the participle ending.

examples.de: Ich habe in der Fabrik gearbeitet.
examples.why: No move from A to B: haben.
A move from A to B: sein.
A move from A to B: sein.

steps: Find the verb.
Ask: does someone move from A to B?
Yes: use sein. No: use haben.

rows: Did I move from A to B?

cards.more: The test is like a gate with one guard. The guard asks: did you arrive somewhere new? If you say yes, you go through the Sein gate. If you say no, you go through the Haben gate. Step 1: find the verb. Step 2: ask did I move from A to B. Step 3: yes means sein, no means haben. The guard never asks about the ending of the participle, only about the move.
cards.lead: You now have two helper verbs and six movement verbs. On this card you get a short test that picks the right helper every time.

deeper.text: The test looks at the whole sentence, not only at the verb. Fahren with a destination, like nach Hamburg, shows a move from A to B. A time word first changes nothing: the helper verb stays in part 2, and the test stays the same.

example.de: Gestern bin ich zur Arbeit gegangen.

cards.title: Airport and journeys at work
cards.body: Many jobs are about travel. Learn five words: der Pilot and die Pilotin, der Fahrer and die Fahrerin, der Flughafen, das Flugzeug and die Dienstreise. They help you tell what happened on a trip.

examples.de: Der Pilot ist nach Wien geflogen.

examples.en: The driver went to the airport.

examples.de: Herr Ali ist letzte Woche mit dem Flugzeug nach Berlin geflogen.
examples.en: Herr Ali flew to Berlin by plane last week.
examples.why: Time, how and where all fit in the middle.

cards.more: A trip has a few small parts: who goes, what they travel in, and where to. Pilot and Fahrer are the people who drive the trip. The Flughafen is where planes start, the Flugzeug is the plane, and a Dienstreise is a trip for work. You can add a time word like letzte Woche or letztes Jahr. Step 1: say who. Step 2: say how and where. Step 3: finish with the participle. Unterwegs means on the way, and zurück means back.
cards.lead: You have the grammar. The last card gives you five work words about travel, so you can tell what happened on a trip.

deeper.text: Flughafen is a built word: Flug (flight) plus Hafen (port) makes airport. German makes long nouns by joining short ones, and the last part gives the article: der Hafen, so der Flughafen. Flugzeug is Flug plus Zeug, a thing, and das Zeug gives das Flugzeug.

example.de: Das Flugzeug ist nach Wien geflogen.

lessons.title: sein with change: bleiben, passieren, aufstehen
lessons.goal: Tell what happened and your morning, using sein for changes and separable participles.

grammar.point: Sein is also used for changes of state and for bleiben, werden, passieren. Separable verbs put ge in the middle: aufgestanden, angekommen, eingekauft.
grammar.oneLine: Ich bin um sieben aufgestanden. Sein in part 2, one long participle at the end.

mistake.why: aufstehen shows a change (lying to standing), so the helper verb is sein. The ge goes inside: aufgestanden.

terms.meaning: when something goes from one state to another, like asleep to awake
the participle of a separable verb: the front part stays in front and ge goes in the middle, as in aufgestanden
first, then, after that: words that put events in order

cards.title: Before we start: what happened this morning?
cards.body: A real moment: a friend sees you late and asks, Was ist passiert? You know separable verbs from chapter 6, like Ich stehe um sieben auf. Today you tell what happened in the Perfekt: sein for changes such as waking up, and the ge that goes in the middle of the verb.
steps: You already know: Ich stehe um sieben auf, a separable verb from chapter 6.
New today: sein for changes, and ge in the middle: aufgestanden.
By the end you can: say Ich bin um sieben aufgestanden and tell your morning in order.

examples.why: You know this: a separable verb in the present.
New today: bin + aufgestanden, with ge in the middle.

cards.more: Think of a morning as a film with small scenes: you wake up, you get up, you stay in a traffic jam, you arrive late. None of these scenes is about doing a job. They are about changing: from asleep to awake, from lying to standing. German gives these changes the helper verb sein. Separable verbs add one small trick: the ge slides in between the front part and the rest, so auf plus stehen becomes aufgestanden. You will learn it in small steps, with a table and a simple test.

cards.title: No movement, still sein
cards.body: A few verbs take sein even without movement. Bleiben (to stay), werden (to become) and passieren (to happen) all take sein. Passieren ends in -ieren, so it has no ge-, as in lesson 3: passiert.
cards.more: Think of these three verbs as being about what happens to you, not what you do. You stay where you are. You become ill. Something happens. Nobody drives anywhere, yet the helper is sein. Step 1: learn the three verbs as a small family. Step 2: remember passiert has no ge-, because it ends in -ieren like studiert and telefoniert. Step 3: say each with ist. Extra example: Ich bin müde geworden means I got tired.
cards.lead: In lesson 5 sein meant movement. On this card sein also goes with verbs where nobody travels: bleiben, werden and passieren.

deeper.text: All three verbs describe a state or a change, not an action you do: you stay, you become, it happens to you. A handy idea: sein goes with verbs about where you are or what happens to you. The -ieren verb passieren never adds ge-, so passiert looks like the present form.

cards.title: Waking up and falling asleep
cards.body: Waking up and falling asleep are changes: asleep to awake and back. These verbs take sein: ich bin aufgewacht, ich bin eingeschlafen. The ge sits inside the verb, because auf and ein are separable. The next card explains why.

examples.en: Ben fell asleep on the train.

cards.more: Imagine a light switch. Click: you are awake. Click: you are asleep. A click is a change, and changes use sein. The words aufwachen and einschlafen both describe a click. Step 1: ask is there a click, a change? Step 2: if yes, use sein. Step 3: put the participle last. The ge hides inside the participle: auf-ge-wacht and ein-ge-schlafen. Do not worry about it yet, the next card makes it clear.
cards.lead: You saw that sein can show a change. On this card: waking up and falling asleep, two changes everyone goes through every day.

deeper.text: Sleeping itself takes haben: Ich habe gut geschlafen, from lesson 4. But falling asleep is a change, so it takes sein. Compare the two: you can sleep for hours (haben), but you fall asleep at one moment (sein). That moment is the click.

cards.title: Separable verbs: the ge goes in the middle
cards.body: Separable verbs put ge in the middle: auf + ge + standen = aufgestanden. The front part stays at the front, and the whole participle is one long word at the end. The helper verb still sits in part 2. Pick sein or haben with the test.

examples.why: aufstehen: sein, ge in the middle.

cards.more: Think of the participle as a sandwich. The front part is the top bread, the verb is the filling, and ge is the sauce in the middle. Auf, ge, standen. An, ge, kommen. Ein, ge, kauft. The sandwich stays together in one piece at the end of the sentence. Step 1: find the front part. Step 2: add ge after it. Step 3: add the rest of the verb, in the form you learned. Then pick sein or haben.
cards.lead: You met aufgewacht and eingeschlafen with a ge hiding inside. This card shows the rule: in a separable verb, ge goes between the front part and the rest.

deeper.text: In the present the front part jumps to the end: Ich stehe um sieben auf. In the Perfekt it stays at the front of the participle, as one word: aufgestanden. So the bracket has only two ends: the helper verb in part 2 and one long participle last. Never split the participle.

cards.title: Was ist passiert? A bad morning
cards.body: Five words help you tell a bad morning: der Wecker (alarm clock), der Stau (traffic jam), der Unfall (accident), plötzlich (suddenly) and zu spät (too late). Learn im Stau stecken bleiben (to get stuck in a traffic jam) as one piece: Ich bin im Stau stecken geblieben.

examples.why: zu spät: learn it as one piece.

examples.de: Ich bin im Stau stecken geblieben.
examples.en: I got stuck in a traffic jam.
examples.why: im Stau stecken geblieben: one piece.
Plötzlich first: the helper verb stays in part 2.

cards.more: A bad morning is a little story with a problem and a surprise. The Wecker did not wake you, so you woke up too late. Then came a Stau, and maybe even an Unfall. Plötzlich is the word for the surprise. Step 1: say what happened first. Step 2: add a small word like plötzlich or zu spät. Step 3: finish with sein or haben and the participle. Extra example: Ich habe den Wecker nicht gehört means I did not hear the alarm clock.
cards.lead: You can build the participles now. On this card: five words for telling a bad morning, so you can answer Was ist passiert?

deeper.text: Was ist passiert? is the normal question when something happened. The answer often starts with a time word or with es: Gestern ist ein Unfall passiert. Passieren never has an object, because things simply happen to people. It always uses sein and has no ge-, so the participle looks like the present form: passiert.

cards.title: haben or sein? The full test
cards.body: Run the three questions in order and stop at the first yes. Most verbs end at question 3: haben. Compare Ich habe geschlafen, no change, with Ich bin eingeschlafen, a change.
steps: Does someone move from A to B? Yes: sein.
Is it a change (waking up, falling asleep) or bleiben, werden, passieren? Yes: sein.
Anything else: haben.
cards.more: The guard at the gate now asks three things. First: did you move from A to B? Second: did something change, or did you stay, become or happen? Third: if both answers were no, you go through the Haben gate. Step 1: ask question 1. Step 2: if no, ask question 2. Step 3: if no again, use haben. Most verbs end up at haben, so haben is your safe friend. Sein is the short list.
cards.lead: Lesson 5 gave you a test with one question. Now it grows to three questions, because sein also goes with changes, bleiben, werden and passieren.

deeper.text: Some verbs are busy actions but take haben, because nobody changes place or state: arbeiten, schlafen, essen. When you meet a new verb, ask the three questions before you build the Perfekt. Good dictionaries also show it: look for ist or hat in front of the participle.

example.de: Mein Onkel hat in der Werkstatt gearbeitet.
example.en: My uncle worked in the workshop.

cards.title: Tell a day in order: zuerst, dann, danach
cards.body: Zuerst means first, dann means then, danach means after that. Each one can start a sentence, and the helper verb stays in part 2 with the subject after it. Mix haben and sein as the test says: Zuerst bin ich aufgestanden, dann habe ich gefrühstückt.

examples.en: First I got up at seven.
examples.why: Zuerst in part 1, sein in part 2.

examples.why: Danach in part 1, sein in part 2.

steps: Zuerst bin ich aufgestanden.
Dann habe ich gefrühstückt.
Danach bin ich zur Arbeit gefahren.
cards.more: A story needs a clear order, like steps on a staircase: first step, second step, third step. Zuerst is step one, dann is step two, danach is step three. Each step is its own sentence with its own helper verb and participle. Step 1: write zuerst and your first event. Step 2: write dann and the next event. Step 3: write danach and the last event. Check haben or sein each time.
cards.lead: You can tell single events. The last card links them into a short story with zuerst, dann and danach.

deeper.text: When zuerst, dann or danach is in position 1, the subject moves behind the verb: Dann habe ich ..., not Dann ich habe. This is the same time-first rule you know from lesson 1 and chapter 2. You can say Dann bin ich ... too, whenever the test says sein.

example.de: Danach habe ich einen Kaffee getrunken.
example.en: After that I drank a coffee.

lessons.title: war and hatte: when you do not use the Perfekt
lessons.goal: Tell about the past mixing war, hatte and the Perfekt, ask Wie war ...? and talk about your studies and your results.

grammar.point: The verbs sein and haben do not use the Perfekt in the past. They use war (ich war, du warst, er war, wir waren, ihr wart, sie waren) and hatte (ich hatte, du hattest, er hatte, wir hatten, ihr hattet, sie hatten). All other verbs use the Perfekt.
grammar.oneLine: Gestern war ich müde. Ich hatte eine Prüfung. Ich habe viel gelernt.

mistake.why: For sein you do not build a Perfekt. Use the short word war.

terms.meaning: was (past of sein)
had (past of haben)
the form to say what happened: helper verb + participle

cards.title: Before we start: how was the exam?
cards.body: After an exam your friends ask: Wie war die Prüfung? You met war and hatte in chapter 6. Today you learn the rule. The two verbs sein and haben do not use the Perfekt. They use these two short words. Every other verb keeps the Perfekt bracket.
steps: You already know: Ich habe gestern Tennis gespielt: helper verb in part 2, participle last (lessons 1 to 6 of this chapter)
New today: war and hatte for sein and haben, in all six persons, and when to choose them instead of the Perfekt
By the end you can: tell a story about yesterday, ask Wie war ...? and talk about your studies

examples.why: You know this already. The Perfekt is a bracket: habe in part 2, gespielt at the end.
New today: for sein you use the short word war. No bracket needed.
New today: for haben you use the short word hatte.

cards.more: Imagine two kinds of luggage. Most verbs travel with two bags: the helper verb and the participle. The two small verbs sein and haben travel light. They carry just one bag: war or hatte. So the only thing to decide is: is my verb sein or haben? If yes, one short word. If no, the bracket you already know. In the next cards you learn all the forms.

cards.title: Two short words win
cards.body: To tell about before, most verbs use the Perfekt. But sein and haben are special. They have their own short past words: war and hatte. You do not build a bracket for them. You just swap the verb: Ich bin müde becomes Ich war müde. Ich habe Zeit becomes Ich hatte Zeit.

examples.de: Ich war gestern in der Uni.

examples.why: Time first, the verb stays in part 2.

steps: sein → war
haben → hatte
every other verb → Perfekt (helper verb + participle)
cards.more: Think of a tiny shortcut on a map. The long road is the Perfekt: helper verb, then participle far away at the end. The shortcut is war or hatte, and it only works for two verbs: sein and haben. Step 1: see sein? Take war. Step 2: see haben? Take hatte. Step 3: any other verb? Take the long road. Extra example: Es war schön = It was nice.
cards.lead: You know the Perfekt bracket from lessons 1 to 6. Now a shortcut: two very common verbs do not need it, and the shortcut makes your German shorter and more natural.

deeper.text: Why do sein and haben get shortcuts? Because you use them all the time, so the short forms survived in everyday speech. Germans say war and hatte in spoken language too, not only in books. For most other verbs, speakers prefer the Perfekt when they talk. So you learn exactly what natives do.

cards.title: war: all six forms
cards.body: The verb war changes with the person. Ich and er/sie/es have no ending, just like the modal verbs. Du gets -st, wir and sie get -en, ihr gets -t. The polite Sie is the same as wir: Sie waren.

examples.en: I was at the cinema yesterday.

examples.de: Warst du gestern in der Uni?
Ben und Mira waren im Café.
examples.en: Ben and Mira were in the café.

cards.more: Learn war like a song with six lines. Ich war, du warst, er war, wir waren, ihr wart, sie waren. Step 1: say the song out loud twice. Step 2: notice that ich and er sound the same, just like the modal verbs in chapter 5. Step 3: cover the table and try again. Extra example: Wir waren gestern müde = We were tired yesterday.
cards.lead: Now the first of the two short words in full. Knowing all six forms lets you say where you, your friends and your boss were, and ask others the same.

deeper.text: Notice the same pattern in the next card: ich and er/sie/es are always the same in the past, du ends in -st, wir and sie in -en, ihr in -t. Once you see this pattern for war, you get hatte almost for free. In spoken German people often shorten words, but at A1 write the full form.

example.de: Wir waren am Montag in der Uni.
example.en: We were at university on Monday.

cards.title: hatte: all six forms
cards.body: The verb hatte works the same way. Ich and er/sie/es have no ending. Du gets -st, wir and sie get -n, ihr gets -t. Use it for things you had: time, hunger, an exam, a good grade.

examples.en: Were you hungry? (Did you have hunger?)

cards.more: Hatte is the twin of war. Same song, new words: ich hatte, du hattest, er hatte, wir hatten, ihr hattet, sie hatten. Step 1: remember that haben = to have. Step 2: say the six forms. Step 3: build one sentence: Wir hatten keine Zeit. Extra example: Ben hatte Hunger = Ben was hungry. Watch one trap: hatten and hattet differ by one letter, so say both slowly, twice.
cards.lead: You know war now. Its twin hatte covers everything you had yesterday: time, an exam or hunger. Same pattern, so this card should feel familiar.

deeper.text: English uses two different ideas here: I was hungry (to be) but German says Ich hatte Hunger (to have). Watch out for this. Hunger and Durst are things you have in German, not things you are. Learn Ich hatte Hunger as one piece.

cards.title: Which one? war/hatte or the Perfekt
cards.body: Two questions decide everything. First: is the verb sein or haben? Then use war or hatte. Second: is it any other verb? Then use the Perfekt with a helper verb and a participle. So: Ich war müde, but Ich habe Tennis gespielt.
steps: Is the verb sein or haben? Use war / hatte.
Any other verb? Use helper verb + participle.
cards.more: It is like a door with two buttons. Button 1: the verb is sein or haben. Press it and the short word opens the door: war or hatte. Button 2: any other verb. Press it and you need two parts: a helper verb and a participle. Step 1: look at the verb. Step 2: press the right button. Extra example: Ich habe Pizza gegessen.
cards.lead: Now you know both tools. This card helps you choose the right one in a fraction of a second, which is what you need when you speak.

deeper.text: A little note: Germans sometimes use the Perfekt of sein and haben too (ich bin müde gewesen), especially in the south, but you do not need it at A1. For now keep it clean: sein and haben use war and hatte. If you follow this rule, you will almost always sound right and natural.

example.de: Gestern war ich in der Uni.

cards.title: Mix them in one story
cards.body: A real story mixes both. Gestern hatte ich eine Prüfung. Ich habe viel gelernt. Es war schwer, aber ich habe bestanden. New verb: bestehen means to pass. It starts with be-, so there is no ge-: hat bestanden.

examples.de: Es war schwer, aber ich habe bestanden.
examples.en: It was hard, but I passed.
examples.why: war for sein; bestanden is a Perfekt participle.

steps: Set the scene: Gestern hatte ich eine Prüfung.
Say what you did: Ich habe viel gelernt.
Say the result: Es war schwer, aber ich habe bestanden.
cards.more: Telling a story is like switching between two tools in a toolbox. Short sentence about how things were: war or hatte. Sentence about something you did: Perfekt. Step 1: set the scene with war or hatte. Step 2: tell the actions with the Perfekt. Step 3: finish with the result. Extra example: Ich war müde, aber ich habe gearbeitet. Now tell your own yesterday in three sentences.
cards.lead: You can choose the right tool for each verb. Now you use both in one little story, the way real speakers do when they tell about a day.

deeper.text: Look at bestanden. It starts with be-, like bezahlt in lesson 3, so there is no ge-. But the stem also changes: bestehen, bestanden. Treat bestanden as one new piece. You will meet more verbs like this, so just learn the participle with the verb: besteht, hat bestanden.

example.de: Ich habe die Prüfung nicht bestanden.
example.en: I did not pass the exam.

cards.title: Past questions
cards.body: Past questions follow patterns you know. With war and hatte the verb is first, or right after the W-word. With other verbs the helper verb is in part 2 and the participle is last. In der Mensa means in the university canteen.

examples.why: Perfekt: helper in part 2, participle last.

cards.more: A question is a normal sentence with the verb moved forward. Step 1: take Du warst in der Mensa. Step 2: move the verb to the front: Warst du in der Mensa? Step 3: for the Perfekt, only the helper verb moves: Du hast gearbeitet becomes Hast du gearbeitet? The participle stays at the end. Extra example: Wo warst du? = Where were you?
cards.lead: You can already tell about the past. Now you learn to ask about it, so you can chat with a classmate about exams, work and yesterday.

deeper.text: Wie war ...? is the most useful past question for daily life. It is how Germans ask for news: Wie war der Urlaub? Wie war dein Tag? Wie war das Seminar? A short answer is enough: Gut! or Es war toll! This is the question you will hear most after an exam.

cards.title: Study life
cards.body: Words for your life at university. Learn each with its article: das Studium, das Seminar, die Note, der Stundenplan, das Referat, der Studiengang, der Abschluss. Also: die Mensa (canteen) and nebenbei (on the side, for example a job next to your studies).

examples.why: Spaß machen: you know this phrase.

examples.en: I work in a café on the side.
examples.why: nebenbei: next to the main thing.

cards.more: Think of your university day as a small town. The Stundenplan is the map: it tells you where to go. The Seminar and the Referat are the places and tasks. The Note is the prize. The Abschluss is the finish line. Step 1: learn each word with its article. Step 2: say one sentence. Extra example: Mein Stundenplan ist neu = My timetable is new.
cards.lead: Now some words for talking about your own studies. They help you fill the sentences you just learned with real, useful content.

deeper.text: Das Studium is almost always singular (the plural Studien is rare). When you say you study, you can say Ich habe Informatik studiert, or you talk about the Studium as a whole. Studiengang is the exact programme, like Informatik or Medizin: your Studiengang is the road, the Abschluss is the goal.

example.en: The degree programme is computer science.
