lessons.title: Applications: your CV in the Perfekt, questions, nicht and schon
lessons.goal: Write a short application email, say what you did, studied and worked, ask and answer past questions, and talk about seasonal jobs.

grammar.point: In Perfekt questions the helper verb comes first (yes/no) or right after the W-word, and the participle stays last. Nicht stands right before the participle: Ich habe nicht gearbeitet. Schon means already, noch nicht means not yet.
grammar.oneLine: Hast du schon gearbeitet? Ich habe nicht gearbeitet. Noch nicht.

mistake.why: The participle must stay at the very end. Nicht goes right before it.

terms.meaning: not: it stands right before the participle
already / not yet
helper verb first, participle last

cards.title: Before we start: apply for a summer job
cards.body: Mira wants a summer job. In chapter 7 you wrote a formal email with Sehr geehrte Frau Weber and Mit freundlichen Grüßen. Today you add the past: what you did and where you worked. You also learn Perfekt questions and where nicht goes.
steps: You already know: a formal email (chapter 7) and the Perfekt bracket: Ich habe gestern Tennis gespielt
New today: Perfekt questions, nicht before the participle, schon and noch nicht, and the words of an application
By the end you can: write a short application email and answer questions about what you did

examples.why: You know this already. Helper verb in part 2, participle last.
New today: in a question the helper verb moves to the front. The participle stays last.
New today: nicht stands right before the participle.

cards.more: An application is like telling a story about yourself in tiny pieces. Each piece is one sentence with the bracket: where you worked, what you studied, what you did. A boss may ask you questions back, so you also need the question form. Step 1: say it. Step 2: ask it. Step 3: say no with nicht. All three use the same bracket you already know.

cards.title: The bracket in a yes/no question
cards.body: In a yes/no question the helper verb moves to the front. The participle stays at the very end. Statement: Sie haben gearbeitet. Question: Haben Sie schon gearbeitet? A short answer: Ja, ich habe gearbeitet. Or: Nein, noch nicht.

examples.why: Object in the middle, participle last.

examples.de: Ja, ich habe in der Werkstatt gearbeitet.
examples.en: Yes, I worked in the workshop.
examples.why: A full answer is a normal Perfekt sentence.

cards.more: A yes/no question is like flipping a coin: only the first two things swap places. Step 1: take the statement Du hast gearbeitet. Step 2: move the helper verb to the front: Hast du gearbeitet? Step 3: leave the participle at the end, where it waits. Extra example: Sind Sie nach Berlin gefahren? = Did you go to Berlin? Say each pair aloud once.
cards.lead: You know the Perfekt bracket as a statement. Now you learn to turn it into a question, which is the first thing a boss or a classmate will ask you.

deeper.text: In a job talk you often hear the formal Sie: Haben Sie schon gearbeitet? Sind Sie schon geflogen? The pattern is the same as with du: helper verb first, participle last. The Sie form always has a capital S, and the helper verb has the same form as for wir: haben, sind.

example.de: Haben Sie schon eine Stelle gefunden?
example.en: Have you found a job already?

cards.title: W-questions in the Perfekt
cards.body: For a W-question put the W-word first. Then comes the helper verb, then the subject, and the participle goes last. Was hast du gemacht? Wo hast du gearbeitet? Wann bist du gekommen? Wie lange hast du gearbeitet?

examples.why: wann asks for a time; kommen uses sein.
wie lange asks for a time span.

cards.more: A W-question is a yes/no question with a question word in front. Step 1: start from Hast du gearbeitet? Step 2: put the W-word before it: Wo hast du gearbeitet? Step 3: the helper verb is still in second place and the participle is still last. Extra example: Was hast du gestern gemacht? = What did you do yesterday? Say all four questions aloud once.
cards.lead: Yes/no questions are done. Now W-questions, so you can ask for details: what, where, when and how long. They are the questions that keep a conversation going.

deeper.text: In an interview you will hear these four questions again and again: Was haben Sie studiert? Wo haben Sie gearbeitet? Wann haben Sie angefangen? Wie lange haben Sie gearbeitet? Learn them as a set. The helper verb is always in second place, even after a long W-word like wie lange.

cards.title: Time first, nicht and schon
cards.body: You can start with the time. The helper verb stays in part 2: Gestern habe ich nicht gearbeitet. Nicht stands right before the participle: Ich habe das Buch nicht gelesen. Schon means already. Noch nicht means not yet: Hast du schon gegessen? Noch nicht.

examples.why: Time first: helper verb still in part 2.

examples.de: Ich habe das Buch nicht gelesen.
examples.en: I did not read the book.

steps: Build the sentence: Ich habe gearbeitet.
Put nicht right before the participle: Ich habe nicht gearbeitet.
schon = already (Hast du schon gegessen?), noch nicht = not yet
cards.more: Nicht is like a stop sign, and it likes to stand right in front of the participle. Step 1: build the sentence: Ich habe gearbeitet. Step 2: find the participle at the end. Step 3: put nicht just before it: Ich habe nicht gearbeitet. Schon is a happy word (already), noch nicht is its sad answer (not yet). Extra example: Ich habe noch nicht gegessen = I have not eaten yet.
cards.lead: Now you can say what you did and ask about it. Next you learn to say what you did not do, and to talk about something that is already done or not yet done.

deeper.text: Noch nicht is also a whole answer. A friend asks: Hast du schon gegessen? You can say just: Noch nicht. In a longer sentence, noch nicht stands before the participle too: Ich habe noch nicht gearbeitet. Nicht and noch nicht take the same place, right before the participle at the end.

cards.title: Your CV in sentences
cards.body: A CV (der Lebenslauf) is a list of things you did. In a talk, say it in short sentences with the Perfekt. Where did you work? What did you study? What did you do? Do not use years yet. Say letztes Jahr (last year) instead.

examples.de: Letztes Jahr bin ich nach Berlin gefahren.
examples.en: Last year I went to Berlin.

steps: Where did you work? Ich habe im Café gearbeitet.
What did you study? Ich habe Informatik studiert.
What else did you do? Ich habe ein Praktikum gemacht.
cards.more: Imagine your CV as a train with one carriage per sentence. Every carriage looks the same: Ich habe, then what, then the participle. Step 1: pick a fact: I worked in a café. Step 2: put habe in second place. Step 3: put gearbeitet at the end. Next carriage: Ich habe Informatik studiert. Extra example: Ich habe in der Werkstatt gearbeitet.
cards.lead: You can ask and answer questions in the Perfekt. Now you put several answers together into a short CV, one sentence per fact.

deeper.text: Germans like a CV that is clear and short. Two or three sentences with the Perfekt are enough for A1: where you worked, what you studied, one thing you did last year. Start with the most important fact. Time words like letztes Jahr or im Sommer can stand in first place, and then the subject follows the verb.

example.de: Im Sommer habe ich im Hotel gearbeitet.
example.en: In summer I worked in the hotel.

cards.title: A job ad and its words
cards.body: An ad for a job is a Stellenanzeige. Often just Anzeige. It asks for Erfahrung (experience) or an Ausbildung (training). You send your Lebenslauf (CV) and your Zeugnis (certificate) with your Bewerbung (application). A student job is a Nebenjob.

examples.en: I would like a side job.
examples.why: möchte + a noun, you know it from food.

cards.more: Think of the application as a small parcel. In the parcel: your Lebenslauf (the story of your life), your Zeugnis (the paper that proves it) and a short letter, the Bewerbung. The Stellenanzeige is the address on the parcel: it tells you where to send it. Step 1: learn the seven words with their articles. Step 2: say one sentence. Extra example: Ich habe eine Bewerbung geschrieben.
cards.lead: You can already talk about the past. Now you learn the words you find in a job ad and in an application, so you can read a Stellenanzeige and understand it.

deeper.text: A Zeugnis is any certificate that shows what you learned or did: a school certificate, a work reference or a diploma. In Germany employers like to see a Zeugnis next to your Lebenslauf. The plural is die Zeugnisse. The Ausbildung is a training of two to three years at a company and a school, and it is very common in Germany.

cards.title: A short application email
cards.body: A short application email has four steps. Greet. Say what you read. Say what you want. Say what you did. Then end politely. Ihre Anzeige means your ad (formal, with capital I). Bei Ihnen arbeiten means to work at your company: learn it as a piece.

examples.en: I would like to work for you.

examples.de: Ich habe schon im Café gearbeitet.
examples.en: I have already worked in a café.
examples.why: schon before the rest, participle last.

steps: Sehr geehrte Frau Weber,
ich habe Ihre Anzeige gelesen.
Ich möchte bei Ihnen arbeiten.
Ich habe schon im Café gearbeitet.
Mit freundlichen Grüßen (new line) Mira
cards.more: An application email is like a small recipe with four steps. Step 1: say hello politely: Sehr geehrte Frau Weber. Step 2: say what you read: Ich habe Ihre Anzeige gelesen. Step 3: say what you want: Ich möchte bei Ihnen arbeiten. Step 4: say what you did and say goodbye: Mit freundlichen Grüßen. Each step is one short sentence you already know. After your email, a Bewerbungsgespräch (job interview) may follow.
cards.lead: You have the words and the sentence patterns. Now you put them in the right order to build a real, short email to a possible boss.

deeper.text: Keep the email short and polite. The words Sehr geehrte and Mit freundlichen Grüßen are the frame of every formal email, and they stay the same. For a man you write Sehr geehrter Herr Ali, with -er at the end. Put your name under Mit freundlichen Grüßen. The boss decides in a few seconds, so short is good.

cards.title: Seasonal jobs in Germany
cards.body: Many students in Germany have a Nebenjob. In summer farms need an Erntehelfer for Spargel (asparagus) and Erdbeeren (strawberries). Hotels and cafés also need extra people for the Saison. A Nebenjob is a good way to earn money next to your studies.

examples.de: Im Sommer arbeite ich als Erntehelferin.
examples.en: In summer I work as a harvest helper.

examples.de: Ich habe im Sommer im Hotel gearbeitet.
examples.en: I worked in the hotel in summer.
examples.why: Perfekt with two small groups before the participle.

steps: Nebenjob = a job next to your studies
Erntehelfer/in = harvest helper (Spargel, Erdbeeren)
Saison = the time of the year when a job exists
cards.more: Seasonal work is work that only exists in one time of the year. The farm needs help when the strawberries are ripe. The hotel needs help when guests come in summer. Step 1: ask: when is the Saison? Step 2: apply for a Nebenjob in that time. Step 3: tell your story with the Perfekt: Ich habe im Hotel gearbeitet. Extra example: Ich bin Erntehelfer = I am a harvest helper.
cards.lead: Now a little culture. What kind of job can a student really get in Germany? This card shows typical Nebenjobs, so your sentences have real content.

deeper.text: Seasonal jobs are popular because they are short and the pay is often fair. The word Saison comes from French and is also used for fashion, sport and tourism. Typical in Germany: Spargel in spring, Erdbeeren in early summer, and a hotel job in the summer holidays.

lessons.title: On the phone: open, ask again, spell, close (and the sound h)
lessons.goal: Take part in a short phone call: open it, say who you are, ask the other person to repeat or spell, close it politely, and say the sound h.

grammar.point: Polite requests use the modal bracket: Können first and the infinitive at the very end (Können Sie das bitte wiederholen?). Phone news uses the Perfekt: Ich habe Sie nicht verstanden (verstehen has no ge-: hat verstanden).
grammar.oneLine: Können Sie das bitte wiederholen? Ich habe Sie nicht verstanden.

mistake.why: Können is first, bitte comes after the person and what you mean, and the second verb goes to the very end.

terms.meaning: polite request: Can you ...?
understood (participle of verstehen, no ge-)
h after a vowel is not pronounced, it only makes the vowel long

cards.title: Before we start: the phone rings
cards.body: On the phone you cannot see the other person, so a few fixed phrases help a lot. In chapter 5 you said Hier ist Leon and Auf Wiederhören. In chapter 7 you asked Können Sie bitte ...? Today you open a call, ask again, spell a word and close the call. You also learn the sound h.
steps: You already know: Hier ist Leon, and the modal bracket (chapter 5): the modal in part 2, the other verb last
New today: Hier spricht ..., Wie bitte?, Können Sie das bitte wiederholen? and Ich verbinde Sie
By the end you can: take part in a short phone call, ask the other person to repeat or spell, and say h correctly

examples.why: New today: the same idea with spricht, the phrase for a call.
New today: a polite request. Können first, wiederholen at the end.

cards.more: A phone call is like a short dance with fixed steps. Step 1: say who you are. Step 2: say what you want. Step 3: if you do not understand, ask again, politely. Step 4: say thank you and goodbye. You already know the bracket for step 3: the modal verb in second place and the other verb at the very end. Today you just fill it with new words.

cards.title: Open a call
cards.body: At the start of a call say hello and your name: Guten Tag, hier spricht Mira. Then say who you want: Ich möchte mit Frau Weber sprechen. The other person may say: Am Apparat. (speaking) or Ich verbinde Sie. (I will put you through). Learn these as whole phrases.

examples.why: Hier spricht ... is the phrase to open a call.

examples.de: Ich möchte mit Frau Weber sprechen.
examples.en: I would like to speak to Mrs Weber.
examples.why: möchte ... sprechen is the bracket you know. Learn mit Frau Weber as one piece.
The answer when you are the right person.
Learn this as a whole phrase.

rows: Ich möchte mit Frau Weber sprechen.
I would like to speak to Mrs Weber.

cards.more: A call has an opening, like opening a door. Step 1: knock with Guten Tag. Step 2: say your name with Hier spricht ... Step 3: say who you want to talk to. The other person has two easy answers: Am Apparat (that is me) or Ich verbinde Sie (I will pass you on). Do not try to explain verbinde. Just learn it like a song line. A phone call is der Anruf: Der Anruf ist für Sie.
cards.lead: You know how to greet someone face to face. On the phone you need a few extra fixed phrases, so you sound clear and polite from the first second.

deeper.text: Why Hier spricht Mira and not Ich bin Mira? On the phone Germans say Hier spricht ... or Hier ist ... instead of I am. It is a fixed habit: hier means here, the place of the speaker. It is also polite to give your full name at a business call. In a private call Hier ist Leon is enough.

cards.title: Ask again
cards.body: If you did not understand, say Wie bitte? (Pardon?) or Noch einmal, bitte. (Once more, please.) A polite full request uses the modal bracket: Können Sie das bitte wiederholen? Können comes first, wiederholen (to repeat) is last. Also: langsamer sprechen (speak slower), lauter sprechen (speak louder).

examples.why: A short and polite way to ask again.
The modal first, the infinitive last.

cards.more: Asking again is like pressing a rewind button. There are three buttons. Button 1: Wie bitte? Button 2: Können Sie das bitte wiederholen? Button 3: Können Sie langsamer sprechen? Step 1: say Können Sie. Step 2: add what you want. Step 3: put the infinitive last: wiederholen or sprechen. Extra example: Können Sie lauter sprechen? = Can you speak louder?
cards.lead: Sometimes you do not understand on the phone. This card gives you the polite ways to ask the other person to say it again, with phrases you can use at once.

deeper.text: On the phone you cannot read lips, so asking again is normal and nobody minds. The word bitte can stand in different places: Können Sie das bitte wiederholen? or Können Sie bitte langsamer sprechen? In both cases können comes first and the infinitive is at the end.

cards.title: Spell it
cards.body: Names and e-mail addresses are hard to hear. Ask: Können Sie das buchstabieren? (Can you spell that?) or Wie schreibt man das? (How do you write that?). Buchstabieren starts with the sound buch- and ends in -ieren, so there is no ge-: you do not need its participle today.

examples.why: Modal bracket again: buchstabieren is last.

examples.de: Mein Name ist Mira: M, I, R, A.
examples.en: My name is Mira: M, I, R, A.
examples.why: Say the letters one by one.

cards.more: Spelling on the phone is like giving someone building blocks, one by one. Step 1: ask Können Sie das buchstabieren? Step 2: the other person says each letter slowly. Step 3: repeat the letters back to check. Letters in German sound like this: M = em, I = ih, R = er, A = ah. Extra example: Wie schreibt man Hallo? = How do you write Hallo?
cards.lead: After asking someone to repeat, the next thing you often need is spelling. This card gives you the two questions and a way to say your own name.

deeper.text: Spelling is very common in Germany, because many names and street names are long. People often say a name for each letter, like M wie Mira. At A1 it is enough to say the letters one after the other, slowly. A German likes it when you repeat the letters back: it shows you are careful.

cards.title: I did not understand: verstanden
cards.body: To say you did not understand, use the Perfekt: Ich habe Sie nicht verstanden. Verstehen starts with ver-, so there is no ge-: hat verstanden. You can also say what you did: Ich habe Ihre Anzeige gelesen. Ich habe Ihre Nachricht gehört.

examples.why: A phone call often starts from something you read.
A question: the helper verb first.

steps: Say who: Ich habe ...
Say what you did not catch: Sie / das
Say nicht + participle: nicht verstanden
cards.more: This is a small copy of lesson 3 and lesson 8. Verbs that start with ver-, be- or er- have no ge-. So verstehen gives verstanden, like bestehen gave bestanden. Step 1: say Ich habe. Step 2: say what you did not catch: Sie. Step 3: nicht, then the participle: Ich habe Sie nicht verstanden. Extra example: Ich habe das nicht verstanden = I did not understand that.
cards.lead: Asking again is polite. You can also tell the other person why you ask: I did not understand. This card shows the Perfekt for that, using the bracket you know.

deeper.text: Verstehen has a small detail: the stem changes in the participle (verstehen, verstanden), just like bestehen, bestanden. You only need to learn the participle with the verb: versteht, hat verstanden. In everyday speech people say Ich habe das nicht verstanden or short: Das habe ich nicht verstanden.

cards.title: Close a call
cards.body: At the end of a call say thank you: Vielen Dank. If nobody answers, you hear a Mailbox (voicemail): Hier ist die Mailbox von Frau Weber. You can say you will call again: Ich rufe später noch einmal an. Always end with Auf Wiederhören! (not Auf Wiedersehen, because you do not see each other).

examples.de: Ich rufe später noch einmal an.
Hier ist die Mailbox von Frau Weber.
examples.en: This is the voicemail of Mrs Weber.
examples.why: Learn von Frau Weber as a piece.

steps: Say thank you: Vielen Dank.
Say what happens next: Ich rufe später noch einmal an.
Say goodbye: Auf Wiederhören!
cards.more: Ending a call is like closing a door softly. Step 1: say thank you: Vielen Dank. Step 2: say what happens next: Ich rufe später noch einmal an. Step 3: say goodbye: Auf Wiederhören! Think: hören is hearing. On the phone you only hear each other, so you say Wiederhören and not Wiedersehen. Extra example: Danke, auf Wiederhören! = Thanks, goodbye!
cards.lead: You can open a call, ask again and spell. Now you close it politely, and you know what to say when you only reach a voicemail.

deeper.text: Wiederhören is only for the phone, radio or other places where you only hear. Wiedersehen means seeing again and is for face to face. Germans pay attention to this small difference. On a Mailbox you can say your name, why you called and that you call again later.

cards.title: The sound h
cards.body: At the start of a word h is a soft breath, like a sigh: Hallo, hier, hören, Haus. After a vowel the h is silent. It only makes the vowel long: gehen, sehen, Uhr, Zahn. So you hear the h in Hallo, but not in gehen.

examples.why: Hallo, hier, Herr: you breathe the h.
gehen and Uhr: the h is silent.
sehe: silent h. Haus: breathed h.

headers: h at the start: a breath

cards.more: Say h like the fog on a window when you breathe on it. At the start of a word: breathe out softly, Hallo. In the middle after a vowel: do nothing. Just make the vowel longer: geeen, seeen. Step 1: breathe on your hand and say Hallo. Step 2: say gehen and feel that no air comes out at the h. Extra example: Uhr (clock) sounds like the English oo-r.
cards.lead: Now for pronunciation. On the phone the other person only hears you, so a clear h helps to be understood, especially in words like Hallo, hier and hören.

deeper.text: The h also appears in some very common words where you do not hear it: nehmen, sehen, gehen, Zahn, Uhr. You can still use it as a clue for spelling: when the vowel is long, a silent h often follows. Native speakers do not have to think about it. You can learn the words as pairs of sound and spelling.

cards.title: A whole call
cards.body: Here is a whole call. Mira phones Frau Weber about the Nebenjob. She opens the call, says why she calls, asks him to repeat, asks him to spell and closes the call. Read the five steps in order and notice the phrases from this lesson.

examples.de: Wie bitte? Ich habe Sie nicht verstanden.
examples.en: Pardon? I did not understand you.

steps: Mira: Guten Tag, hier spricht Mira.
Mira: Ich habe Ihre Anzeige gelesen.
Mira: Wie bitte? Ich habe Sie nicht verstanden.
Mira: Können Sie das bitte buchstabieren?
Mira: Vielen Dank. Auf Wiederhören!
cards.more: A call is a story with five short scenes. Scene 1: Mira opens. Scene 2: she says why she calls. Scene 3: she does not understand and asks again. Scene 4: she asks for the spelling of the mail address. Scene 5: both say goodbye. Step 1: read the five lines. Step 2: cover them and say them from memory. Step 3: swap the names and make your own call.
cards.lead: You have all the pieces now. Putting them together into one call shows you how the phrases follow each other when you really use them.

deeper.text: Real calls are never perfect, so use the phrases you have like tools. If you get lost, say Wie bitte? If a name is hard, say Können Sie das buchstabieren? If it gets too fast, say Können Sie langsamer sprechen? Three tools are enough to survive a first call in German and keep the talk polite.
